'''Richard Milton Martin''' (12 January 1916, [[Cleveland, Ohio]] &ndash; 22 November 1985, [[Milton, Massachusetts]]) was an American [[logician]] and analytic [[philosopher]].

In his Ph.D. thesis written under [[Frederic Brenton Fitch|Frederic Fitch]], Martin discovered virtual sets a bit before [[Willard Van Orman Quine|Quine]], and was possibly the first non-Pole other than [[Joseph Henry Woodger]] to employ a [[mereology|mereological]] system. Building on these and other devices, Martin forged a [[first-order logic|first-order theory]] capable of expressing its own [[syntax]] as well as some [[semantics]] and [[pragmatics]] (via an [[event logic]]), all while abstaining from [[Set (mathematics)|set]] and [[model theory]] (consistent with his [[nominalist]] principles), and from [[intension]]al notions such as [[modal logic|modality]].

== Life and career ==
Richard Milton Martin was born on January 12, 1916 in Cleveland, Ohio to Frank Wade Martin and Lena Beatrice (Bieder).<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/whoswhoinamerica0002unse/page/2165/mode/1up |title=Who's who in America |publisher=[[Marquis Who's Who]] |year=1980 |isbn=978-0-8379-0141-1 |edition=41st 1980–1981 |volume=2nd |location=Chicago |page=2165 |url-access=registration |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>

From [[Harvard University|Harvard]], where he had studied under [[Alfred North Whitehead]] during his last year before retirement,<ref name=":0" /> Martin earned an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] in 1938.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last= |url=https://archive.org/details/contemporaryauth15lind/page/305/mode/1up |title=Contemporary authors new revision ser vol 15 a bio-bibliographical guide to current writers in fiction, general nonfiction, poetry, journalism, drama, motion pictures, television |publisher=[[Gale (publisher)|Gale]] |year=1985 |isbn=978-0-8103-1944-8 |editor-last=Metzger |editor-first=LInda |page=305 |url-access=registration |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>

He then obtained an M.A. from [[Columbia University|Columbia]] (1939), and his Ph.D. from [[Yale University|Yale]] (1941).<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Kline |first1=George |author-link=George Kline |last2=Silber |first2=John |author-link2=John Silber |date=1986 |title=In Memoriam: Richard M. Martin (1916–1985) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20128376 |journal=[[The Review of Metaphysics]] |volume=39 |issue=3 |jstor=20128376 |issn=0034-6632 |url-access=registration }}</ref> His dissertation, supervised by.logician [[Frederic Fitch]],<ref name=":0" /> was on “A Homogeneous System for Formal Logic.”<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Anellis |first=Irving H. |title=Dictionary of Modern American Philosophers, 1860–1960 |publisher=Thoemmes Press, [[Continuum International Publishing Group|Continuum]] |year=2005 |editor-last=Shook |editor-first=John R. |chapter=Martin, Richard Milton (1916–1985) |isbn=978-1-84371-037-0 |author-link=Irving Anellis |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ijpj1tB3Qr0C&pg=PA1628}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Martin |first=R. M. |date=1943 |title=A Homogeneous System for Formal Logic |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2267976 |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.2307/2267976 |jstor=2267976 |issn=0022-4812 |url-access=registration |quote=A part of the material of this paper was contained in a thesis, of the same title, presented for the degree Doctor of Philosophy in Yale University, 1941. The author wishes to thank Professor Frederic B. Fitch for many invaluable criticisms and suggestions... }}</ref>

He was an instructor in mathematics at [[Princeton University]] 1942&ndash;44, then at the [[University of Chicago]] 1944&ndash;46.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> He then taught philosophy at [[Bryn Mawr College]] 1946&ndash;48, the [[University of Pennsylvania]] 1948&ndash;59, the [[University of Texas at Austin|University of Texas]] 1959&ndash;63 and at [[New York University]] 1963&ndash;73.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> From 1973 until his retirement in 1984 he taught at  [[Northwestern University]], Martin also held visiting appointments at [[University of Bonn|Universitact Bonn]], Yale, [[University of Hamburg|Universitact Hamburg]], the [[The New School for Social Research|New School for Social Research]], and [[Temple University]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

In 1976, Martin largely retired from teaching (only giving one course per year at Northwestern from then on) becoming a research associate with [[Boston University Center for Philosophy and History of Science|Boston University Center for the Philosophy and History of Science]]. He made excellent use of the resulting leisure, so that his final decade of life was by far his most productive, publishing over 100 book chapters and journal articles.<ref name=":0" />

He published what Meguire describes as "the definitive treatment of his logic"<ref name=":0" /> within ''Semiotics and Linguistic Structure'' (1978). The next year saw the publication of his edited volume of the writings of [[Carolyn Eisele]] on [[Charles Sanders Peirce]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dauben |first=Joseph W. |author-link=Joseph Dauben |date=March 1982 |title=Studies in the Scientific and Mathematical Philosophy of Charles S. Peirce: Essays by Carolyn Eisele. Carolyn Eisele, R. M. Martin |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/352961 |journal=Isis |language=en |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=143–144 |doi=10.1086/352961 |issn=0021-1753 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

He also helped edit, and contributed chapters to, the ''[[Festschrift]]en'' books ''The Logical Enterprise'' (1975)<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/logicalenterpris0000unse |title=The Logical Enterprise |publisher=Yale Univ. Press |year=1975 |isbn=978-0-300-01790-8 |editor-last=Anderson |editor-first=Alan Ross |editor-link=Alan Ross Anderson |location=New Haven |url-access=registration |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> dedicated to Fitch, and ''Studies in the Philosophy of J. N. Findlay'' (1985).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cohen |first1=R. S. (Robert Sonné) |url=http://archive.org/details/studiesinphiloso00cohe |title=Studies in the philosophy of J.N. Findlay |last2=Martin |first2=R. M. (Richard Milton) |last3=Westphal |first3=Merold |author-link3=Merold Westphal |date=1985 |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |isbn=978-0-87395-795-3 |location=Albany |url-access=registration |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> (Having been a colleague of [[John Niemeyer Findlay|J. N. Findlay]] at Austin, Texas.)<ref name=":3" />

At the time of his death, Martin served on the editorial board of eight journals and on the advisory board of the Peirce Edition Project. In 1981, he became president of the Charles S. Peirce Society. In 1984, he was elected president of the [[Metaphysical Society of America]], and he delivered their presidential address at [[Vanderbilt University]] in March 1985.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Martin |first=R. M. |date=1985 |title=On the Metaphysical Status of Mathematical Entities |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20128277 |journal=The Review of Metaphysics |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=3–21 |jstor=20128277 |issn=0034-6632 |url-access=registration }}</ref>

Despite having held tenure track appointments from 1948 until his retirement in 1984, the only Ph.D. thesis known to have been completed under Martin’s supervision is that of James Scoggin. Otherwise, Martin’s legacy is coextensive with his published writings.

Martin died at his home in Milton, Massachusetts, on November 22.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Anon. |date=March 1986 |title=In Memoriam  |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2041-6962.1986.tb00445.x |journal=[[The Southern Journal of Philosophy]] |language=en |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=147 |doi=10.1111/j.2041-6962.1986.tb00445.x |issn=0038-4283 |url-access=subscription |quote=With deep regret we report the death of one of our Editorial Board members,  Richard M. Martin, who died at his home in Milton, Massachusetts, on November 22, 1985. Richard Martin published fifteen books and nearly 150 articles ranging over an extraordinarily wide variety of topics and philosophers. ...  He  was a  contributor to many Festschriften including those for Y. Bar-Hillel, Fr. J. M. Bochenski, John N. Findlay, Frederick Fitch, Nelson Goodman, Charles Hartshorne, Sidney Hook, and Paul Lorenzen, and to the Library of Living Philosophers volume on Carnap. He was a consulting editor for a number of journals in addition to this one. |via=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hiż |first=Henry |author-link=Henryk Hiż |date=1986 |title=Richard M. Martin † |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/kant.1986.77.1-4.271/html |journal=[[Kant-Studien]] |publisher=[[De Gruyter]] |volume=77 |issue=1–4 |pages=271–272 |doi=10.1515/kant.1986.77.1-4.271 |issn=0022-8877 |url-access=subscription |via=}}</ref>

== Ideas ==
"...one of the most many-sided, prolific, and scholarly of analytic philosophers."
:&mdash;Hans Burkhardt, Foreword to ''Metaphysical Foundations: Mereology and Metalogic''.

Martin was part of the first wave of American analytic philosophers; arguably, only Quine (1908&ndash;2000), Fitch (1909&ndash;1987), and [[Henry Leonard (philosopher)|Henry Leonard]] (1905&ndash;1967) preceded him. His chronological elders [[Nelson Goodman]] (1906&ndash;1998) and [[Wilfrid Sellars]] (1912&ndash;1989) were arguably his contemporaries, as they all began their careers in earnest at about the same time, namely right after World War II. Martin's formal treatment of syntax followed [[Alfred Tarski]]; of semantics, [[Rudolf Carnap]]. Martin was generally well-disposed towards Carnap's work, contributed a long paper to the Schilpp volume on Carnap, and was seen as a disciple. Paradoxically, Martin was a [[positivism|positivist]] and radical [[nominalism|nominalist]] who also sympathized with [[process theology]] and orthodox [[Christianity]].

Between 1943 and 1992, Martin published 16 books and about 240 papers (of which 179 were included in his books) on an extraordinary range of subjects, including [[aesthetics]], logic, the [[foundation of mathematics]], [[metaphysics]], [[syntax]]/[[semantics]]/[[pragmatics]], the [[philosophy of science]], [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]], [[process philosophy]], [[theology]], [[Frege]], and C.S. Peirce. Martin preached and practiced that philosophy should be done formally, by employing first-order logic, the theory of [[virtual set (mathematics)|virtual set]]s and [[Relation (mathematics)|relations]], and a multiplicity of [[Predicate (logic)|predicate]]s, all culminating in an [[event logic]]. Starting with the papers reprinted in his 1969 ''Belief'', Martin argued that the Frege's ''Art des Gegebensein'' was crucial to his thinking. Just what this ''Art'' entailed remains to be elucidated.

Martin was especially fond of applying his first-order theory to the analysis of ordinary language, a method he termed ''logico-linguistics''. He often referenced the work of the linguists [[Zellig Harris]] (admiringly) and [[Henryk Hiż|Henryk Hiz]] (more critically); Martin, Harris, and Hiz all taught at Pennsylvania in the 1950s. Yet Martin was dismissive of the related theoretical work by [[Noam Chomsky]] and his MIT colleagues and students. Ironically, Martin appears to have been Chomsky's main teacher of logic; while a student at Pennsylvania, Chomsky took every course Martin taught.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Meguire |first=Philip |date=1 January 2005 |title=Richard Milton Martin: American Logician |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/review-of-modern-logic/volume-10/issue-1-2/Richard-Milton-Martin-American-Logician/rml/1203432181.full |journal=The Review of Modern Logic |volume=10 |issue=31 |pages=7–65 |via=[[Project Euclid]] |accessdate=24 April 2014}}</ref>

Quine's ''[[Word and Object]]'' cites Martin with approval, but Martin's wider impact has not been commensurate with the breadth and depth of his writings; the secondary literature on Martin consists of little more than reviews of his books.

== Quotations ==
“Over the portals of the entrance to contemporary philosophy is writ: Enter here fully equipped with the tools of the new logic.” ''Intension'', p.&nbsp;153.

“God made first-order logic and all the rest is the handiwork of man.” ''Semiotics'', p. xv.

== Works ==
The first four titles below and the first part of ''Semiotics'' (1978) are monographs. The other titles are fairly loose collections of papers, most first published in journals.

* 1958. ''[[iarchive:truth00mart|Truth and Denotation: A Study in Semantical Theory]]''. University of Chicago Press.
* 1959. ''[[iarchive:towardsystematic0000mart|Toward a Systematic Pragmatics]]'' (Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics). Greenwood Press.
* 1959. ''The Notion of Analytic Truth''. University of Pennsylvania Press.
* 1963. ''[[iarchive:intensiondecisio00martrich|Intension and Decision]]''. Prentice-Hall.
* 1969. ''[[iarchive:beliefexistencem0000mart|Belief, Existence, and Meaning]]''. New York University (NYU) Press.
* 1971. ''[[iarchive:logiclanguagemet00rmma|Logic, Language, and Metaphysics]]''. NYU Press.
* 1974. ''[[iarchive:whiteheadscatego0000mart|Whitehead's Categorial Scheme and Other Papers]]''. Martinus Neijhoff.
* 1978. ''[[iarchive:eventsreferencel0000mart|Events, Reference, and Logical Form]]''. Catholic University of America Press.
* 1978. ''[[iarchive:semioticslinguis0000mart|Semiotics and Linguistic Structure]]''. State University of New York (SUNY) Press.
* 1979. ''Pragmatics, Truth, and Language''. Reidel.
* 1979. ''Peirce's Logic of Relations and Other Studies''. Boston Studies in the Philosophy of Science. [[John Benjamins Publishing Company|John Benjamins]].
* 1980. ''[[iarchive:primordialitysci0000mart|Primordiality, Science, and Value]]''. SUNY Press.
* 1981. ''Logico-Linguistic Papers''. Foris (Netherlands).
* 1983. ''[[iarchive:mindmodalitymean0000mart|Mind, Modality, Meaning, and Method]]''. SUNY Press.
* 1988. ''Metaphysical Foundations: Mereology and Metalogic''. Philosophia Verlag.
* 1992. ''Logical Semiotics and Mereology''. John Benjamins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Misiuna |first=K |date=3 April 2007 |title=R, M. Martin, Logical semiotics and mereology. (Foundations of Semiotics, 16.) Amsterdam and Philadelphia:John Benjamins Publishing Company, 1992, xiii + 282pp. $79 DM150 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01445349508837245 |journal=History and Philosophy of Logic |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=134–136 |doi=10.1080/01445349508837245 |issn=0144-5340 |quote=The book .., is a collection of essays … that ... may be read separately. What is characteristic of Martin's philosophy, and ... exposed here, is an opposition to set theory. Martin argues that set theory is to be rejected because of its excessive ontic commitment, and replaced by a theory ... able to provide foundations for mathematics avoiding dubious assumptions ... This conviction takes the form of a philosophical programme ... to be accomplished ... by a quite original theory ... known as ordinal mereology (OM) or omogeneous logic (HL), where only individuals are admitted as values for variables. Sets and classes, excluding virtual classes and relations which may be regarded as a ''façon de parler'', are to be gratuitous entities, since 'the only entities that should be needed are those that are needed ''überhaupt'' in science and elsewhere; the admission of sets is at best an ''ad hoc'' device  within mathematics alone' (p. 134).|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
A complete bibliography of Martin's articles published in journals, conference proceedings, and  books edited by others can be found in Meguire, Philip, 2005.<ref name=":0" />
